1

Welcome and sign in

Five steps from first open to the first trip. A finished profile skips straight to Discover; a half-finished one resumes at step 3.Psychology: Explore before any account; sign-in counts as step 1, so the profile starts at 2 of 4; name and photo come from Google.

2

Discover

The swipe deck, the Reels toggle, sending a trip to a chat, empty states, and the full filter screen.Psychology: Faces of who’s going on every card, seat counts that are true, one action per card, and empty states that always offer a next step.

3

Trip and booking

From the trip page to a paid seat. The host shows as a first name and a verified tier until you have paid.Psychology: The group and safety come before the itinerary, the total and the free-cancel date come before Pay, UPI is the default, and “You’re in” is the peak of the app.

4

My trips

Four tabs for booked, saved, past and cancelled trips, with the booking, cancel and review sheets and the payments history.Psychology: The next trip sits on top with a countdown and pack list, every finished trip gives a magnet, and cancelling shows the refund and an alternative first.

5

Chats and notifications

The Chats tab, every thread type, the info screens and their sheets, and the notifications list.Psychology: Trip groups show how soon the trip is, the host opens with an intro round, and empty states point back to trips.

6

You

Your profile, other people’s profiles, editing, followers, and creating and saving reels.Psychology: Profile progress says what’s missing and why the group cares; magnets turn past trips into a collection.

7

Settings

Grouped rows, switches, and the pages behind them. Settings sits behind the gear on your profile.Psychology: Calm, with no primary button. Leaving shows exactly what you lose and offers hiding your profile instead.

8

Why it’s built this way

The rules used on every screen, what we refused, and the research.

Rules on every screen

  • One gradient action per screen. Two primaries means no primary.
  • Seat counts, deadlines and refunds are always true and agree across screens.
  • Empty and error states always offer a next step. No dead ends.
  • The ask comes after the value: browse free, sign in at the first save.
  • Totals, taxes and the free-cancel date show before Pay.

What we refused

  • Viewer counts like “12 people are looking”.
  • Timers that reset, or prices that “go up tonight” when they don’t.
  • Rewards that depend on a good review.
  • Pre-ticked add-ons at checkout.
  • Guilt-trip buttons when cancelling or deleting.

Needs your decision

  • Guest browsing needs the API to allow reading trips without a session.
  • Gender mix and ages on the trip need profile data and an opt-out.
  • “Same-gender tents only” is a host policy, not just UI.
  • Trip home, pack list, magnets and trip alerts are new features.
  • Icons still missing: food, wellness, budget, people.

Sources

  • Baymard, checkout UX benchmark: about 70% of carts are abandoned; extra costs and forced accounts are top reasons.
  • Baymard, mobile checkout: 60% of test users overlooked a buried guest option.
  • Lazyweb, guest mode by vertical: 9 of 18 travel apps let people browse before sign-up.
  • Curology case: delaying account creation lifted conversion 22% (self-reported).
  • Ert, Fleischer & Magen 2016: trustworthy-looking host photos raised bookings more than review scores.
  • Outlook Traveller survey: women ask first about safety, stays and room partners.
  • RBI via Free Press Journal: UPI was 85.5% of payment volume in H2 2025.
  • Outside, trip countdown and Topdeck: countdowns, checklists and pre-trip group chats as the pre-trip hook (no hard retention data found).
  • SAP Fiori and Atlassian on empty states: say why it’s empty and give the next action.
  • Subsets on pause flows: offer an alternative before the exit (vendor data, optimistic).
  • More in design-ref/ui-psychology.md.

Design preview. Photos are Unsplash and faces are placeholders. Names, prices and dates are sample data in the same shape the app uses.
